subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: expecting the new place to feel like home instantly [Pitfall]
passage:
Counsellor's note, Jahnavi, hostel wing.
Sarthak arrived in July saying he would have a hundred friends by Friday. In the third week he sat in my office and said everyone else already belonged, that he was the only lonely one, and that he wanted to go home and drop out. I asked what he had expected, and he said, “I thought it would feel like home in a few days.” I told him that adjusting to a new place usually takes months, and that feeling lonely in week three is common, not a verdict on him. We wrote one small thing for each day: sit at a different mess table, say hello to one person, walk to the library with the floor. He agreed to see me on Friday and to tell his parents how he feels, without deciding anything about leaving yet. I will check in weekly.

qa.q: In which week did Sarthak say he wanted to drop out?
qa.a: In the third week, Sarthak said he wanted to go home and drop out.

qa.q: What was Sarthak feeling when he sat in the counsellor's office?
qa.a: Sarthak felt panicked and lonely, thinking everyone else already belonged and that he was the only lonely one.

qa.q: What different way of thinking could help Sarthak, and why?
qa.a: Expecting adjustment to take months and taking one small social step each day, because it makes the loneliness a normal phase rather than proof that he does not fit.

qa.q: How might Sarthak's parents feel when he tells them how he feels?
qa.a: They may feel worried and want to help, but hearing it plainly lets them support him without rushing a decision about leaving.

grounding: A student assumes he will fit in within days, feels panicked and lonely by week three and wants to drop out, not knowing adjustment takes months.
